lede: A courier rides out with a parcel and comes back past the depot. She has covered plenty of ground, and she has not ended up far from where she started. Average speed measures the ground. Average velocity measures the ending up.
can: Find the total distance and the total displacement of a journey.
Divide by the total time, waiting time included.
Say which of the two a question wants, and give the sign.

md: Average speed asks how much ground was covered. Average velocity asks how far the object ended up from where it started. A courier who rides out and comes back past the depot has a large average speed and an average velocity of almost nothing. Both divide by the **total** time, waiting included.

md: Follow the picture and two different totals come out of it. The bike covers $180 + 240 = 420$ m of road: that is the **distance**. It finishes 60 m past the depot on the far side, so its **displacement** is $-60$ m. Same journey, two honest answers to two different questions.

prompt: Work out the total distance the bike covers, in metres.
explain: 180 m out and 240 m back: $180 + 240 = 420$ m of road covered.

alt: A table of four words: distance is every metre covered so it only grows; displacement is where it ended up with its sign; average speed is total distance divided by total time; average velocity is total displacement divided by total time.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 439 210' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='439' height='210'><rect x='2' y='2' width='435' height='206' rx='8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-opacity='0.5'/><path d='M6 76H433M6 106H433M6 136H433M6 166H433M6 196H433M156 46V196' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.8' stroke-opacity='0.45'/><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><text x='12' y='35' font-size='13.5' font-weight='600'>Four words, kept apart</text><text x='12' y='65' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>Word</text><text x='162' y='65' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>What it means</text><text x='12' y='95' font-size='13'>distance</text><text x='162' y='95' font-size='13'>every metre covered, so it only grows</text><text x='12' y='125' font-size='13'>displacement</text><text x='162' y='125' font-size='13'>where it ended up, sign included</text><text x='12' y='155' font-size='13'>average speed</text><text x='162' y='155' font-size='13'>total distance ÷ total time</text><text x='12' y='185' font-size='13'>average velocity</text><text x='162' y='185' font-size='13'>total displacement ÷ total time</text></g></svg>
caption: Same denominator, different numerator.

md:
**Average speed** $= \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$ and **average velocity** $= \dfrac{\text{total displacement}}{\text{total time}}$.

The bike takes $40 + 20 + 60 = 120$ s, so its average speed is $420 \div 120 = 3.5$ m/s and its average velocity is $-60 \div 120 = -0.5$ m/s. One journey, one clock, two answers that are not even the same sign.

prompt: Work out the average velocity of the bike, in m/s.
explain: Displacement $-60$ m over 120 s gives $-0.5$ m/s. The minus sign says it ended up on the far side of the depot.

caption: The 20 seconds at the door are part of the journey.

md: The time underneath is the whole journey, from the first second to the last. Waiting counts, because the bike really did take 120 seconds to do what it did. Leaving the stop out would describe a journey that never happened, and it always makes the answer too big.

title: What an average speed is really saying
md: It answers one question: if the whole journey had been done at a single steady speed, what would that speed have been? Every second between the start and the finish belongs underneath, whether the body was moving or not.

prompt: A van drives for 240 s, waits for 60 s and drives on for 300 s. What total time goes underneath, in seconds?
explain: $240 + 60 + 300 = 600$ s. Using 540 s would leave the wait out and make the average speed too big.

caption: A ferry crossing 900 m, waiting, then coming back.

md:
**Distance:** $900 + 900 = 1800$ m, because the ferry really did cross twice.
**Time:** $150 + 30 + 180 = 360$ s, the wait included.
**Average speed:** $1800 \div 360 = 5$ m/s.
**Displacement:** the ferry finishes where it began, so it is $0$ m, and the average velocity is $0 \div 360 = 0$ m/s.

prompt: A swimmer swims six lengths of a straight 25 m pool in 250 s. What is her average speed, in m/s?
explain: Six lengths is $6 \times 25 = 150$ m, and $150 \div 250 = 0.6$ m/s. Her average velocity is 0, because she finishes at the end she started from.

title: Speed, Distance and Time
why: The arithmetic underneath, done slowly. Watch how the units are fixed before the division rather than after it.

md: A cyclist rides 400 m at 8 m/s and then 400 m at 4 m/s. It is very tempting to write 6 m/s.

prompt: You have two minutes left and a two-mark average-speed part. What do you write first?
options: The total distance and the total time, on two lines
answer: The total distance and the total time, on two lines
explain: Those two lines carry the method mark even if the division then goes wrong, and an unsupported answer earns nothing in Further Mathematics.

md: It is not 6. The first stretch takes 50 s and the second takes 100 s, so she spends twice as long going slowly. Her average speed is $800 \div 150$, about $5.33$ m/s. Averaging two speeds is safe only when the stages take the same time, so work from the totals every time.

prompt: A lorry drives 2400 m in 240 s, stops for 60 s, then drives 1500 m in 300 s. What is its average speed?
explain: 3900 m over 600 s. The 7.5 comes from averaging 10 and 5; the 7.22 comes from leaving the 60-second stop out of the time.

alt: A table of conversions: 1.5 km is 1500 m; 5 minutes is 300 s; 36 km per hour is 10 metres per second, dividing by 3.6; 12 metres per second is 43.2 km per hour, multiplying by 3.6.

md:
If the answer line prints m/s, every length must be in metres and every time in seconds before anything is divided. Kilometres with seconds gives a number a thousand times too small.

The first two rows are the ones FM2 asks for.

title: km/h is not FM2 content
md: The last two rows are useful, not examined. The letters km appear nowhere in the FM2 papers from 2018 to 2026, and the specification has no unit-conversion statement: m/s to km/h is a GCSE Mathematics skill. Metres and seconds are the units of this unit.

title: You can now
md:
Find a total distance and a total displacement from a journey or a graph.
Divide by the whole time, waiting included.
Say which of the two a question wants, and give its sign.
Change kilometres to metres and minutes to seconds first.
Say why averaging two stage speeds fails.

title: Sheet or memory?
md:
**On the Unit 2 formula sheet:** nothing for this topic.
**Must be known:** average speed = total distance ÷ total time; average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time; speed is the size of the velocity and is never negative; waiting time counts; fix the units first.

prompt: A runner runs 600 m out and 600 m back in 300 s. Which pair is right?
options: Average speed $4$ m/s, average velocity $0$ m/s
Average speed $0$ m/s, average velocity $4$ m/s
Average speed $4$ m/s, average velocity $4$ m/s
answer: Average speed $4$ m/s, average velocity $0$ m/s
explain: 1200 m covered gives a speed of 4 m/s. She finishes where she started, so her displacement, and with it her average velocity, is zero.

md:
Find the total distance and the total displacement of a journey.
Divide each by the total time, waiting time included.
Say which of the two the question wants, and give the sign.

A two-mark instruction to calculate an average speed, often straight after a graph you have just drawn. The first mark is a correct total distance or total displacement; the second is the division by the whole journey's time. Stuck: write the total distance over the total time as a fraction, waiting time included.
